content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.9, after using 28 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L2-S2-M2. Then I tested tasks chosen so the two hypotheses predict different results. The free `compare` command gave each test task's overlap with the trained tasks, measured as the share of inputs where the responses match.

| Test task | New rules | Overlap with trained tasks | Mean examples needed (individual results) |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S2-M2 | 0 | 0.06 | Before training: 60 (65, 55). After: **14** (1, 28, 10, 31, 14, 1) |
| L1-S1-M3 | 1 | 0 | **28** (33, 28, 35, 17) |
| L3-S3-M3 | 3 | 0 | **35** (51, 43, 23, 36, 52, 5) |
| L4-S3-M4 | 3 | 0.56 | **37** (29, 40, 40, 17, 49, 47); before training: 48 (37, 58) |

**Why this points to part-based:**
- **Familiar rules, almost no overlap:** L1-S2-M2's mapping barely matches either trained task, yet it became much cheaper to learn. That fits part-based and is what a holistic learner should not do.
- **New rules, different overlap:** The two tasks with three new rules cost about the same, although one overlaps 0.56 with a trained task and the other 0. A holistic learner would have found the overlapping one easier.
- **One new rule:** L1-S1-M3 landed in between, consistent with cost rising with the number of new rules.

**Caveats:** The noise is large, with single results ranging from 1 to 52, and each condition has only 4–6 samples. L4-S3-M4 also had only two tests before training. Even so, the main gap (14 vs. about 36) is consistent and well beyond the spread, so I set confidence at 0.9 rather than higher.
